verdict:
This is a dual-timeline domestic ghost story set in Renick, West Virginia. Ellen, a court reporter in her fifties, buys an old house and reconstructs the 1983 death of its former owner, Della Markey, through county records, probate files, a coroner's inquest, and — ultimately — Della's household ledger. Alternating with that investigation are chapters in Della's voice, looping through the night she died: stove cold, chimney failed, her estranged brother Cale knocking at the front door while she sat with the travel clock and did not go down. The book's fidelity frame is the procedural accuracy of official documents, and its central argument — that a sentence read without its surrounding paragraph is not the certified record — is thematically sound and felt.

Against that frame the verisimilitude largely earns its keep. The draft-reversal mechanism for an exterior chimney in sustained extreme cold is technically correct and is cross-confirmed between Della's remembered knowledge of it, her father's teaching, and the coroner's finding of no mechanical defect. The chain of title, the probate administration procedures, the coroner's inquest format, the depositions that bookend Ellen's professional life: all convincingly realized. The household ledger as discovered artifact is the book's most impressive sustained consistency achievement — the hand transition from Harold to Della in October 1975, the dwindling of Cale's appearances to October 1979, the storm-preparation entries of January 1983, the cold-hands pressure visible in the final entry — all hold precisely when Ellen finally reaches them.

The most significant failures are in the numbered documents, which is exactly where they do the most damage. The pathologist's time-of-death window shifts between chapters: Ellen copies it verbatim from the report in chapters 9 and 11 as 10 PM–4 AM, but cites the same report in chapter 21 as "2–5 AM." This matters to the book's argument: Ellen uses the later window to calculate "four or more hours" of survival after Cale's knocking; the earlier window she had already recorded would not support that calculation. The indoor temperature on the same night at approximately 8:30 PM is 51°F in chapters 2 and 4 (where it is derived from an explicit thermometer reading) and 39–40°F in chapters 12 and 16 (where the same character reads the same thermometer). Mabel Duff's witness statement changes substantively between chapters: "evening of February tenth" in chapter 11 becomes "morning of February 10th" in chapter 21; an entire paragraph about Mabel trying the front door is absent from the chapter-21 quotation; and chapter 23 places Mabel's testimony as referring to "14 Verrill Street" — a dropped digit, the address throughout the novel being 412. For a book whose entire thematic engine is the difference between a verbatim record and a paraphrase, these errors at the level of the very documents the plot depends on are not small.

There is also an unresolved contradiction that Ellen — a professional court reporter trained to notice precisely this kind of thing — does not flag: Mabel Duff's own statement says "I tried the door, which was unlocked," while Deputy Harman's statement and the investigation report both confirm the front door was deadbolt-locked from the inside. A reader who has absorbed Ellen's professional habits will notice this; the narrative does not.

strongest.claim: The exterior-chimney draft-reversal mechanism is technically accurate and is triangulated between Della's embodied knowledge (her father's teaching), her own failed attempts to prime the flue, and the coroner's finding of 'no mechanical defect' alongside 'consistent with draft reversal during sustained periods of extreme cold.' The distinction between a device that has not broken and a condition that has made it unable to function is precise and consequential.

The chain of title and probate research is procedurally convincing. Grantor-grantee indexing, the distinction between testate and intestate succession, the quit-claim as an inter-family transfer before death, the eight-year administrative limbo when an heir cannot be located — all are accurately rendered and integrated into the plot without feeling like research showing.

The ledger as discovered artifact is the novel's sustained consistency achievement. The hand transition from Harold to Della in October 1975, the dwindling of Cale's appearances across the 1970s, the October 1979 last entry under his name, the January 1983 storm preparation, and finally the final entry written in 'cold hands' — all cohere precisely on first and second reading. The revelation earns what the preceding investigation has built.

Ellen's court-reporter discipline is consistently embodied as an epistemological method: she reads documents in order, marks inaudible passages rather than filling them in, and identifies the difference between 'failure of heating source' (the inquest verdict's language) and 'no mechanical defect' (the investigation's finding). The analysis of Della's last sentence as 'an excerpt' that the surrounding paragraph governs is intellectually coherent and genuinely earned.

The material world of the 1983 night — the Riverside range, the single-pipe steam radiators, the oil lamp wick-trimming, the travel clock wound by radio — is specific and period-plausible throughout the Della chapters, and the accumulation of small physical facts (the third step's flex, the north-wall window frost patterns) gives the ghost narrative a concrete grounding that earns its strange quality.

weakest.claim: The pathologist's time-of-death window contradicts itself across chapters. In chapters 9 and 11 Ellen copies it from the report as 'sometime between 10:00 p.m. on the evening of February 11 and 4:00 a.m. on the morning of February 12, 1983.' In chapter 21 the same report yields 'TOD est. 2–5 AM, Feb 11-12' — a completely different window, starting four hours later and ending one hour later. Ellen uses the chapter-21 window to calculate that Cale's knocking ended 'four or more hours' before Della's death; the chapter-9 window would make that calculation wrong. This is a direct contradiction in the novel's pivotal forensic document.

Mabel Duff's witness statement is not stable across readings. Chapter 11 quotes her saying 'I last saw Miss Markey on the evening of February tenth'; chapter 21's photocopy version has her saying 'I saw Della at her mailbox on the morning of February 10th.' The paragraph in which Mabel says 'I tried the door, which was unlocked' — present in the chapter-11 original — is absent from the chapter-21 quotation. Chapter 23 renders Mabel's testimony as covering 'the residence at 14 Verrill Street' rather than the established 412 Verrill Street. The variation in time of day (evening vs. morning) and the dropped door paragraph look like revision artifacts not reconciled across chapters.

The indoor temperature at approximately 8:30 PM on the night of February 11 is given irreconcilable values. Chapter 4 states 'The wall thermometer reads forty-four degrees. Seven degrees since half past eight' — placing the half-past-eight temperature at 51°F, consistent with chapter 2's explicit reading of 51°F at 8:42 PM. Chapter 12 states 'forty when I checked it again at half past eight'; chapter 16's retrospective ledger reading gives 'Temperature at half past: thirty-nine.' The same thermometer on the same night reads either 51°F or 39–40°F at 8:30 PM — a twelve-degree gap that cannot be reconciled by narrative structure.

The front door is simultaneously locked and unlocked at the time of discovery. The coroner's investigation report and Deputy Harman's statement both confirm that the front door 'was locked — a deadbolt, noted as engaged from the inside,' requiring entry through a defective kitchen window latch. Mabel Duff's own witness statement says 'I tried the door, which was unlocked, and I could see from the threshold that something was wrong.' These accounts cannot both be accurate, and Ellen — introduced to us as a professional whose job is catching exactly this kind of discrepancy — never flags it.

The matches shift location across chapters without explanation. Chapter 2 places 'twelve' matches in a box on the shelf above the stove. Chapter 6 has Della open 'the tin from my coat pocket' and find three. Chapter 12 asserts 'the two matches are in the tin in the drawer to the left of the sink, where they have always been kept in this house' — a claim that flatly contradicts the shelf location in chapter 2. Chapter 14 moves them back to 'the tin on the kitchen shelf.' The 'always been kept' assertion in chapter 12 is particularly jarring because it is stated as settled fact about the house's habits, not as narrative movement.

quotes.text: She wrote: *failure of heating source / no mechanical defect* and drew a line between them in her notebook.
quotes.why: The book's precision at its best: Ellen registers that the inquest verdict's language ('failure of heating source') and the investigation's finding ('no mechanical defect') are two different claims about the same event, and that the paraphrase has absorbed a distinction the mechanism requires. This is the epistemological argument in miniature.

quotes.text: sometime between 10:00 p.m. on the evening of February 11 and 4:00 a.m. on the morning of February 12, 1983
quotes.why: Ellen copies this from the pathologist's report 'exactly as it appeared.' Chapter 21 cites the same report as 'TOD est. 2–5 AM, Feb 11-12' — a four-hours-later start time. The window Ellen uses to anchor her final conclusions is not the window she first recorded.

The contradicting version of the same pathologist's window. Ellen uses this figure to calculate 'four or more hours' of survival after the knocking stopped at 9:52 PM — a calculation the chapter-9 window (10 PM–4 AM) would not support.

quotes.text: The wall thermometer reads forty-four degrees. Seven degrees since half past eight.
quotes.why: Places the temperature at half past eight as 51°F. Chapter 2 confirms 51°F at 8:42 PM on the same night. Chapter 12 states the temperature at half past eight was 40°F — a twelve-degree contradiction on the same physical thermometer.

quotes.text: The front door was locked — a deadbolt, noted as engaged from the inside.
quotes.why: The investigation report and Harman's statement both confirm this. Mabel Duff's statement in chapter 11 says 'I tried the door, which was unlocked' — a direct contradiction in the same file that Ellen reads as a professional transcriptionist and never flags.

quotes.text: the two matches are in the tin in the drawer to the left of the sink, where they have always been kept in this house
quotes.why: The 'always been kept' claim is made as settled house history, but chapter 2 puts the matches in a box on the shelf above the stove; chapter 6 finds them in Della's coat pocket. Three locations across three chapters, with the chapter-12 version asserting permanence.

quotes.text: no visitors to the residence at 14 Verrill Street
quotes.why: A dropped digit. The house address is established as 412 Verrill Street in chapter 1 and confirmed across the entire chain of title. '14' is a production artifact in the chapter that is otherwise the novel's most careful synthesis of its documentary record.

who_is_this_for: Readers who respond to quiet, procedural fiction in which archives and official records mediate access to silenced lives — the kind of reader who stays with Elizabeth Strout's domestic accumulations or who reads W.G. Sebald for the documents rather than despite them. The ghost-story element is never confirmed and never explained; readers who need resolution in the uncanny will be unsatisfied. The West Virginia setting is specific and unsentimental: this is not Appalachian Gothic but Appalachian bureaucracy, which is a rarer and more interesting register.
